phases.message: We've never kept up with drawback. Start here in Portline: read the rules, every import line we paid duty on, and the claims we've already filed.
Now Forwarden. Go through this year's exports and check the proof that each one actually left the country.
This is our Ledgerline ERP. Trace every export back to what it shipped and where each part came from, using the bills of materials.
And Docshelf, our trade folder. Read whatever bears on which exports can be claimed.
Back in Portline. File a drawback claim for every export that qualifies, designating the right import lines, at 99% of the duty to the cent. Then tell me what you left out and why.

rules.text: Today is Friday 9 October 2026. Drawback refunds duties paid on imports that leave the United States (19 U.S.C. 1313; 19 CFR Part 190). Topics: unused, manufacturing, time, designation, amount, proof. One claim per export, filed through Portline into CBP's ACE.

1313(j)(1), unused merchandise: imported, duty-paid goods exported within five years of their import and not used in the United States before export. Testing, inspecting and repacking are not use; goods put into service here, such as a rental fleet's, have been used. The claimant must be the importer of record, or hold a certificate of delivery from the importer: goods bought from a US distributor carry no drawback for the buyer without one.

1313(a), manufacturing: articles made in the United States from imported, duty-paid merchandise and then exported. It needs a manufacturing drawback ruling. Designate the imported components the work order consumed, unit for unit, by import line (direct identification). Domestic components carry no duty to refund.

A claim must be filed within five years of the import date of the merchandise it designates (1313(r)(1)). After that it is abandoned: an import of 3 March 2021 could be claimed until 3 March 2026, and not after.

Each imported unit can be designated on one claim only, and an export that supported one claim cannot support another (1313(v)). Portline shows how many units of each import line earlier claims designated; a line with none left cannot be designated again.

Drawback is 99% of the duties, taxes and fees paid on the designated imports (1313(l)(2)(B)): units x paid per unit x 0.99, summed over the import lines, to the cent. A line entered duty-free has nothing to refund.
An export is proven by the Electronic Export Information's ITN, or a bill of lading showing the goods left the United States. A booking cancelled before departure is not an export.

documents.title: Manufacturing drawback ruling: letter of notice
documents.text: CBP acknowledged Quillon's letter of notice on 2020-05-11 under the general manufacturing drawback ruling for pump assembly (19 CFR 190.7). It covers QP-series pumps made from imported housings, motors and seal kits, with records kept by direct identification, lot by lot.

documents.title: Ohio Motor Supply: purchase terms
documents.text: M-75 motors bought from Ohio Motor Supply, a US distributor that imports them itself. Ohio Motor Supply gives no certificate of delivery and transfers no drawback rights to buyers.

documents.title: Rental fleet policy
documents.text: Motors moved from inventory into the rental fleet become fixed assets. They run in rental pumps at customers' sites in the United States until retired or sold.

documents.title: Importer of record
documents.text: Quillon Pumps, Inc. is the importer of record on every entry filed under filer code QPW by its customs broker, and pays the duties itself.
